claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite containing discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments in a Cu matrix.
The starting W–Cu composite has phase separation and interfacial voids.
A brief nanosecond-pulse laser treatment will be targeted at W/Cu interfacial regions.
Nanosecond-pulse laser irradiation will produce rapid local heating at the interfaces.
The laser treatment will locally remelt and rapidly resolidify the W–Cu interfaces.
The laser pulses will momentarily melt Cu adjacent to W.
Transient melting and rapid resolidification will refine the W/Cu interfacial microstructure.
The treatment will create a void-free W/Cu interface with enhanced metallurgical bonding.
Fast cooling after laser heating will homogenize the phases at the W/Cu interface.
Laser processing will eliminate interfacial microvoids and phase separation.
Eliminating interfacial voids and improving bonding will reduce interfacial thermal resistance.
Untreated phase separation and interfacial voids act as barriers to heat conduction.
The laser-treated W–Cu composite will have higher effective thermal conductivity than the untreated composite.
The laser-treated composite will have improved durability under simulated thermal cycling and irradiation.
The proposed treatment is applicable under cyclic high-heat-flux and irradiation conditions representative of W-based plasma-facing material/Cu-based cooling-component joints.
Laser fluence, pulse duration, and scanning parameters must be optimized for the intervention to be effective.
Optimization can avoid overheating and bulk degradation of the W–Cu composite.
The treatment's benefits are limited to composites whose interfacial length scale is amenable to rapid remelting and resolidification.
The optimal laser parameters and the long-term irradiation stability of the modified interface are uncertain.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant void-fraction reduction or a measurable conductivity improvement relative to an untreated control would falsify the hypothesis.
